title: Losar
hookLine: the Tibetan new year: cleaning the house, new prayer flags, fresh starts

cards: In Tibetan homes, a few days before the new year, everybody grabs a broom. Corners get scrubbed. Old dust goes out the door.

It closes a week of festivals: the hungry ghosts fed, monks inviting each other to name their faults, a robe sewn in a single day, the Buddha coming down from heaven, the morning star, the passing between the sal trees.
Yesterday ended with an ending. So today the calendar turns over. Today is Losar.

teach.b: Losar is two Tibetan words: lo, year, and sar, new. It follows the Tibetan lunar calendar, so it moves, usually landing in February or early March.
It's kept in Tibet and by Tibetans everywhere, and in Bhutan, Ladakh and the Himalayan communities of Nepal, sometimes on different dates.

First comes the cleaning: in the last days of the old year, houses are cleaned top to bottom. On the twenty-ninth evening, many families eat a soup called guthuk, with dough balls hiding little objects inside.
Find salt and you're said to be lazy; find chili and you're said to have a sharp tongue. Everyone laughs.
Then leftover soup and a dough figure are carried out of the house, with the old year's troubles, and left at a crossroads. Next, the flags.
Strings of prayer flags, blue, white, red, green and yellow, are printed with prayers and mantras, and over a year wind and sun fade them to rags.

At Losar many families take down the old ones and hang new ones on rooftops and passes. In Tibetan custom, the wind carries the blessings printed on them out to every being it touches. Then the visits.
Monasteries hold special rituals and masked dances.
Families visit shrines, make offerings, and greet each other with tashi delek, good fortune.

Many historians think parts of Losar are older than Buddhism in Tibet, and that Buddhist practice and those older customs grew up together. Losar takes yesterday's line seriously, and then picks up a broom.
The old year is really over, so you clear it out, and begin.

how: Tibetan Buddhist families prepare for Losar by cleaning their homes, then hang new prayer flags, visit monasteries and shrines, make offerings and visit relatives over the first days of the new year.

o: the Tibetan day of the dead

p: soup with hidden objects in the dough

s: it follows the Tibetan lunar calendar, usually in February or early March.
old prayer flags are often replaced with new ones at Losar
the faded flags come down and fresh ones go up.
every custom of Losar began with Buddhism
historians trace parts of it to older seasonal festivals in Tibet.

games.q: it's the twenty-ninth evening. you bite into your guthuk dumpling and find a chili inside. what happens?
o: you have to leave the table.
everyone laughs: a sharp tongue, they say.
you get to make a wish.
games.why: the hidden objects are a family joke: chili means a sharp tongue, salt means lazy. then the old year's troubles are carried out.

practice: Picture one corner of your home, one drawer or one shelf, and what's piled there from a year that's already gone. In your mind, lift each thing, wipe the dust, keep what's useful and let go of what isn't.
Notice the feeling of space when it's done.

wordCard.voice: Losar. The Tibetan new year: lo, year, sar, new. Cleaned houses, new prayer flags, and tashi delek. Today's word.

orig.note: Tibetan lo gsar: lo, year, and gsar, new; written gsar, said sar.

carryVoice: Your line: a fresh year. Old dust out, new flags up. Day six hundred ninety-three, done.
